title: The Crossing
logline: Where a stream has no bridge, people cross by a rope tied to a tree: a run-up, a grip, a swing, an unsteady landing, and then, every time, a moment of standing firm on the far side.
human_question: Is the moment you let go the same moment you are safe, or are those two different things?

situation.what_happens: A community without a bridge crosses a stream every day by rope, log or pole, to reach fields, school or a road. Each crossing has the same shape: a decision, a commitment that cannot be taken back once made, a landing that is always unsteady, and a second afterwards in which the person recovers their footing. In flood the same crossing is a different proposition, and some people stop making it.
situation.who_is_involved: The households on the far side; children going to school; older people who now hesitate or stop crossing; whoever maintains the rope or the log, and whoever is blamed when it is not maintained.
situation.what_is_at_stake: Daily access to work, schooling and help, and sometimes real physical risk. Also the community's standing: a missing bridge is a grievance as well as a fact, and the film can easily make it look picturesque.
situation.how_it_unfolds: The crossing is routine in the dry months and dangerous after rain, and its condition drifts until someone repairs it. Pressure comes from water level, from loads carried, and from people who should not be crossing but must. It ends, in a lifetime, either with a bridge or with someone being hurt. Reality decides what the water does during filming, and no one is ever asked to cross for the camera.

concept_merge.why_together: C100 (path and fruition processes) contributes its own image of the decisive moment: a man runs, grips a rope hanging from a branch, swings over a canal, lets go, and stands on the far bank shaking before he finds his footing [C100-P4:L44–L46]. C098 (the noble persons) contributes what the texts say about the kind of change that happens there: not held down, not displaced, but finished [C098-P4:L205–L249].
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: Together they separate two things a single word usually covers. Letting go is not arriving; the landing is not yet the standing. And the texts' claim that such a change does not come back is thrown into relief by a crossing that has to be made again tomorrow. C100 alone is a vivid image; C098 alone is a classification. The pair asks the viewer to feel the difference between a crossing you repeat and one you do not.

concept_links.why: The sources' own simile for the path moment is a man who runs, grabs a rope, swings over a canal, lets go and stands shaking on the far bank before he finds his footing [C100-P4:L44–L46]. The digest warns this is not an 'aha moment' or a big life decision, so the film keeps the image and makes no equivalence.

What the texts describe as changing at that moment does not come back, unlike what is only suppressed or displaced [C098-P4:L205–L249]. The film's crossings are repeatable by nature, which is an honest, non-equivalent counterpoint rather than an illustration.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: Letting go and being safe are two different moments: you let go of the rope, land shaking, and only then find your footing. The texts use exactly this picture for the decisive change they describe.
what_must_be_real: A crossing people genuinely depend on, filmed as they use it. Nobody is asked to cross, to cross again, or to cross in higher water for the film, and the hardship is not presented as charm.
position_hint: middle: it is the group's first decisive-change film, and it sets up the later distinction between a change that holds and one that has to be made again.
risks: Making the absence of a bridge look picturesque rather than unjust
Safety of anyone filmed crossing, especially children and in high water
Over-explaining the simile in narration until the crossing stops being real work
drop_if: No such crossing can be filmed without encouraging risk
The community does not want a hardship shown

connections.note: From a season of small judgements to a single committed moment.
Both ask whether a change is temporary or final, one through a crossing, one through a root.
The same far-shore question approached through what carries people across rather than through the crossing itself.

selection.reason: Used by EPD-0092; the rope-and-canal image is the sources' own and the film keeps it non-equivalent.

unknowns: No participant or event has been found or confirmed. Everything here is a research direction.
evidence_class_note: Editorial proposal. No location, scene or shot decisions are made at the idea stage.
